passage.title: How Wolves Reshaped the River
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
For nearly seventy years, not a single gray wolf howled in the valleys of Yellowstone National Park. Hunters and rangers had removed the last wolf packs in the 1920s. They thought the park's elk and deer would thrive without wolves. Instead, the elk herds grew so large that they lingered all winter along the flat creek bottoms. Year after year, hungry elk chewed young willow and aspen shoots down to bare stubs before the saplings could grow tall.

Without streamside trees to shade the water and hold the dirt in place, the valley creeks began to suffer. Bare mud banks crumbled into the current when spring snow melted on the peaks. The streams grew wide, shallow, and warm under the summer sun. Beavers vanished from several valleys because they had no tall willow branches to eat or weave into lodges and dams.

In 1995, park scientists brought gray wolves from Canada back into Yellowstone. Right away, the return of these swift hunters changed how the elk used the land. The wolves caught only a small part of the herd. Still, the elk stopped standing for hours in open river bottoms where wolf packs could corner them. Young willow and cottonwood groves, browsed down to the mud for decades by lingering elk herds, were finally given room to recover by the return of hunting wolf packs. Within a few summers, green leafy branches arched six feet above the water.

Taller willow thickets soon sparked a chain of new life along the creeks. Songbirds returned to nest in the dense, shady branches. Best of all, beavers moved back into the valleys to cut the fresh willow stems. One beaver colony grew to nine colonies across the northern range. Their sturdy wood dams slowed the fast spring water and formed deep, cool ponds.

Those beaver ponds acted like sediment traps that healed the worn-out creeks. Silt settled to the bottom of the pools instead of washing downstream, and thick willow roots locked the banks into firm soil. Narrower, deeper channels kept the water cool for native trout all summer long. By bringing back one missing hunter at the top of the food web, scientists proved that wolves could help mend the very shape of a river.

tier2Words.definition: stayed in one place for a long time instead of moving on
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English lengan ('to prolong or stay')
tier2Words.contextClue: Without wolves to chase them, the elk herds stayed all winter along the flat creek bottoms.

tier2Words.definition: young, slender trees that have not yet grown to full height
tier2Words.rootHint: From sap ('young tree juice') + suffix -ling ('small one')
tier2Words.contextClue: Hungry elk chewed young willow and aspen shoots down to stubs before the young trees could grow tall.

tier2Words.definition: fed on leaves, twigs, and young shoots of trees or shrubs
tier2Words.rootHint: Old French brost ('young shoot or twig')
tier2Words.contextClue: For decades, elk herds chewed the young willow and cottonwood shoots down to the mud.

tier2Words.definition: sand, mud, and silt carried by water that settles to the bottom of a pond or river
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root sedere ('to sit or settle')
tier2Words.contextClue: Silt and mud settled to the bottom of the beaver pools instead of washing downstream.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Young willow and cottonwood groves, browsed down to the mud for decades by lingering elk herds, were finally given room to recover by the return of hunting wolf packs."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what had damaged the young tree groves, and what allowed them to recover?

options.text: Hunting wolf packs chewed the willow groves down to the mud, and lingering elk herds helped the trees recover.
Lingering elk herds had chewed the groves down, and the return of hunting wolf packs gave the trees room to recover.
Cottonwood groves chased the hunting wolf packs away from the muddy river bottoms for decades.
Park rangers planted plastic fences around every single willow tree in Canada.

questions.provingSentenceText: Young willow and cottonwood groves, browsed down to the mud for decades by lingering elk herds, were finally given room to recover by the return of hunting wolf packs.
questions.childTip: Check both 'by' phrases: elk herds did the browsing down, while the return of wolf packs gave room to recover.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, the first 'by' phrase ('by lingering elk herds') names the agent that damaged the trees, and the second ('by the return of hunting wolf packs') names what enabled their recovery.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 1:

"Instead, the elk herds grew so large that they lingered all winter along the flat creek bottoms. Year after year, hungry elk chewed young willow and aspen shoots down to bare stubs before the saplings could grow tall."

What does the word lingered mean as it is used in Paragraph 1?

options.text: Stayed in one area for a long time without moving away
Sprinted across the icy creeks as fast as possible
Built tall wooden lodges out of woven willow branches
Migrated hundreds of miles north into Canada every autumn

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead, the elk herds grew so large that they lingered all winter along the flat creek bottoms.
questions.childTip: Compare Paragraph 1 with Paragraph 3, where elk later 'stopped standing for hours in open river bottoms.'
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 notes that elk stayed 'all winter along the flat creek bottoms,' and Paragraph 3 contrasts this by stating they later 'stopped standing for hours' there, confirming 'lingered' means remained or hung around.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why did beavers disappear from several Yellowstone valleys before 1995?

options.text: Gray wolves hunted all the beavers along the northern range in the 1920s.
The creeks froze solid from top to bottom during the hot summer months.
They lacked tall willow branches to eat and use for building their lodges and dams.
Native trout ate all the underwater plants that beavers needed for winter food.

questions.provingSentenceText: Beavers vanished from several valleys because they had no tall willow branches to eat or weave into lodges and dams.
questions.childTip: Click the last sentence of Paragraph 2 that gives the exact reason beavers vanished from the valleys.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 directly explains that beavers vanished from several valleys because overgrazing by elk left no tall willow branches for beavers to eat or weave into lodges and dams.

questions.prompt: Which evidence does the author provide in Paragraph 4 to support the claim that regrowing willow thickets brought new life to the creeks?

options.text: The number of beaver colonies on the northern range grew from one to nine, and songbirds nested in the shady branches.
Park rangers dug nine artificial lakes with bulldozers to hold the spring snowmelt.
Elk herds learned to weave willow branches into shelters to hide from Canadian wolves.
Every single creek in Yellowstone dried up completely within a few summers.

questions.provingSentenceText: One beaver colony grew to nine colonies across the northern range.
questions.childTip: Look in Paragraph 4 for the specific facts and numbers showing which animals returned to the willows.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4 (ELAGSE5RI8), the author supports the claim that taller willows triggered new life by citing returning songbirds and the jump from one beaver colony to nine colonies.

questions.prompt: Part A: How does the author support the idea that returning wolves helped heal the physical shape of Yellowstone's rivers?

options.text: By tracing how wolves kept elk moving, which let willow roots and beaver dams trap silt and narrow the creek banks
By showing that wolf packs dug new river channels with their paws during the spring snowmelt
By proving that beavers only build dams in rivers where no willow trees or cottonwoods grow
By explaining that native trout pushed mud onto the riverbanks to shade the water

questions.provingSentenceText: Silt settled to the bottom of the pools instead of washing downstream, and thick willow roots locked the banks into firm soil.
questions.childTip: Follow the chain from Paragraph 3 to Paragraph 5: wolves moved elk, willows grew, beavers built dams, and roots locked the soil.
questions.parentExplanation: Across Paragraphs 3-5, the author connects the return of wolves to elk movement, willow recovery, beaver dams trapping silt, and roots stabilizing the banks into narrower, deeper channels.

options.text: "For nearly seventy years, not a single gray wolf howled in the valleys of Yellowstone National Park."

questions.provingSentenceText: Silt settled to the bottom of the pools instead of washing downstream, and thick willow roots locked the banks into firm soil.
questions.childTip: Pick the quote in Paragraph 5 that shows how beaver pools and willow roots physically healed the banks.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D directly quotes Paragraph 5, showing the physical mechanism (trapped silt in beaver pools and thick willow roots locking the soil) that reshaped the riverbanks.
